questions.q: From the table above, the equilibrium price before the tax was
questions.explanation: Before the tax, quantity demanded equals quantity supplied (300 bottles) at ₦60.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, the equilibrium quantity traded before the tax was
questions.B: 250 bottles
questions.D: 400 bottles
questions.explanation: At the pre-tax equilibrium price of ₦60, both Qd and Qs1 are 300 bottles.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, at a price of ₦75 before the tax the market would have
questions.B: a shortage of 300 bottles
questions.D: a surplus of 300 bottles
questions.explanation: At ₦75, Qs1 (450) exceeds Qd (150) by 300 bottles, so there is excess supply.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, the equilibrium price after the tax was imposed is
questions.explanation: After the tax, Qd equals Qs2 (250 bottles) at ₦65.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, the part of the ₦10 tax per bottle that is passed on to consumers is
questions.D: nothing
questions.explanation: The price paid by consumers rose from ₦60 to ₦65, so consumers bear ₦5 of the tax and sellers bear the other ₦5.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, the government's weekly revenue from the tax is
questions.explanation: After the tax 250 bottles are sold each week; 250 × ₦10 = ₦2,500.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Using the table above, the price elasticity of demand when the price falls from ₦60 to ₦50 (original values) is
questions.explanation: Quantity rises by 100 from 300 (33.3%); price falls by ₦10 from ₦60 (16.7%); 33.3 ÷ 16.7 = 2.0, so demand is elastic.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, if the government had fixed a maximum price of ₦50 before the tax, the market would have had
questions.B: a surplus of 200 bottles
questions.D: no shortage or surplus
questions.explanation: At ₦50, Qd is 400 but Qs1 is only 200, leaving excess demand of 200 bottles.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Comparing Qs2 with Qs1 in the table above, the effect of the tax on the supply curve is that it
questions.A: was unchanged, but demand shifted to the left
questions.B: shifted to the right, with more supplied at every price
questions.C: became a vertical line at 250 bottles
questions.D: shifted to the left, with less supplied at every price
questions.explanation: At every price Qs2 is 100 bottles less than Qs1: the tax raised sellers' costs and shifted supply leftwards (upwards).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, the marginal utility of the third meat pie is
questions.B: 12 utils
questions.D: 8 utils
questions.explanation: Marginal utility = change in total utility: 48 − 36 = 12 utils.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, the marginal utility of the fifth meat pie is
questions.B: 60 utils
questions.D: 12 utils
questions.explanation: Marginal utility of the fifth pie = 60 − 56 = 4 utils.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The pattern of marginal utility in the table above illustrates the
questions.B: law of diminishing returns
questions.D: law of diminishing marginal utility
questions.explanation: Each extra meat pie adds less satisfaction than the one before (20, 16, 12, 8, 4 utils).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, the number of meat pies the student should buy to maximise satisfaction is
questions.explanation: Buy while the money value of marginal utility (MU × ₦50) is at least the price of ₦500, i.e. MU ≥ 10 utils: pies 1, 2 and 3 (MU 20, 16, 12). The fourth pie is worth only 8 × ₦50 = ₦400.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: If the price of a meat pie in the table above fell to ₦300, the student would buy
questions.B: 3 pies
questions.D: 2 pies
questions.explanation: Now buy while MU × ₦50 ≥ ₦300, i.e. MU ≥ 6 utils: the fourth pie (MU 8, worth ₦400) is bought but the fifth (MU 4, worth ₦200) is not.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, the average utility per pie when four pies are eaten is
questions.B: 56 utils
questions.D: 14 utils
questions.explanation: Average utility = total utility ÷ quantity = 56 ÷ 4 = 14 utils.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: From the table above, total utility keeps rising from the first to the fifth pie but at a decreasing rate because
questions.A: the price of meat pies rises with each one bought
questions.B: each extra pie adds less satisfaction than the one before
questions.C: the student's income falls as she buys more pies
questions.D: the canteen reduces the size of each extra pie sold
questions.explanation: Marginal utility is positive but falling, so total utility rises more slowly with each additional pie.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Economics is regarded as a social science because it
questions.A: uses laboratory experiments to prove every one of its theories
questions.B: studies human choices about scarce resources in a systematic way
questions.C: deals only with the production of goods in factories and on farms
questions.D: is concerned mainly with how governments raise and spend taxes
questions.explanation: Economics studies human behaviour (choice under scarcity) using systematic methods of observation and analysis.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A minister says, "The government SHOULD remove the fuel subsidy in order to save money." This statement is
questions.B: a positive statement
questions.D: a scientific fact
questions.explanation: It expresses an opinion about what ought to be done, which is normative; positive statements describe what is and can be tested.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following is a topic in microeconomics?
questions.A: the growth of the country's total output
questions.B: the rate of inflation in Nigeria
questions.D: the pricing of sachet water in a local market
questions.explanation: Microeconomics studies individual units such as a single market, firm or consumer; the others are economy-wide (macro) issues.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The basic economic question "for whom to produce" is concerned with
questions.A: the choice of technique used in production
questions.B: how output is shared among the members of society
questions.C: the types of goods a country decides to produce
questions.D: the quantity of resources available to producers
questions.explanation: "For whom" is the distribution question; "what" concerns the goods chosen and "how" concerns the method of production.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Bread bought by a family for breakfast is a ______ while the flour bought by the bakery to make it is a ______.
questions.B: producer good; consumer good
questions.D: durable good; capital good
questions.explanation: Goods used directly to satisfy wants are consumer goods; goods used to produce other goods are producer (capital) goods.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Air in the open atmosphere is classified as a free good because it
questions.A: is not needed for any productive activity
questions.B: is provided by the government at no charge
questions.C: cannot be seen or touched by the consumer
questions.D: is available in abundance and commands no price
questions.explanation: A free good exists in such abundance relative to wants that it has no opportunity cost and no price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The work done by a teacher in a classroom is classified in economics as
questions.B: a service
questions.D: a durable good
questions.explanation: Services are intangible economic goods that satisfy wants; they are consumed as they are produced.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The fundamental economic problem facing every society is that
questions.A: the prices of goods rise every year
questions.B: governments never have enough money to spend
questions.C: human wants are unlimited while resources are limited
questions.D: workers are not paid enough for their labour
questions.explanation: Scarcity of resources relative to unlimited wants forces every society to make choices.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: In economics, wealth refers to
questions.A: any item that satisfies a want without any payment
questions.B: the flow of money a person earns within a year
questions.C: the total amount of cash kept in a bank account
questions.D: the stock of valuable goods owned at a point in time
questions.explanation: Wealth is a stock of economic goods (houses, land, machinery, shares) that have value and are owned; income is a flow.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A student's monthly allowance of ₦20,000 is an example of
questions.B: income, which is a flow
questions.D: savings, which is a stock
questions.explanation: Income is measured per period of time (a flow); wealth and capital are measured at a point in time (stocks).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The statement "a rise in the price of rice will reduce the quantity of rice demanded" is positive because it
questions.A: is always true in every country
questions.B: expresses the opinion of consumers
questions.D: was made by a government official
questions.explanation: Positive statements are about what is and can be verified or refuted by facts; they contain no value judgement.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Macroeconomics is concerned with
questions.A: the wages paid to the workers in one small local industry
questions.B: the behaviour of one consumer choosing goods in a single market
questions.C: the pricing decision of a single firm selling one product
questions.D: the economy as a whole, such as total output and the price level
questions.explanation: Macroeconomics studies aggregates: national income, employment, inflation and growth.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A farmer's plot can produce maize worth ₦300,000, cassava worth ₦250,000 or yam worth ₦200,000 in a season. If he grows maize, his opportunity cost is
questions.B: ₦250,000 worth of cassava
questions.D: ₦300,000 worth of maize
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone, which is the cassava.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Scarcity in economics means that
questions.A: a country is poor and most of its people are unemployed
questions.B: goods are not available in the shops during a shortage
questions.C: resources are limited relative to the wants they must satisfy
questions.D: the government has banned the importation of some goods
questions.explanation: Even rich countries face scarcity: resources are never enough to satisfy all wants.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A state government with a limited budget builds a hospital instead of a stadium. The stadium forgone is the
questions.B: money cost of the hospital
questions.D: opportunity cost of the hospital
questions.explanation: The alternative sacrificed when a choice is made is the opportunity (real) cost of that choice.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Choice is necessary in economics because
questions.A: consumers do not know what they want
questions.B: resources are scarce relative to human wants
questions.C: prices are fixed by the government
questions.D: producers make too many kinds of goods
questions.explanation: Since limited resources cannot satisfy every want, individuals and societies must choose which wants to satisfy.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A country producing on its production possibility curve can increase its output of cars only by
questions.B: employing its idle resources
questions.C: reducing its output of the other good
questions.D: raising the price of cars
questions.explanation: On the curve all resources are fully and efficiently used, so more of one good means less of the other.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A point inside a country's production possibility curve indicates
questions.B: full employment of all resources
questions.C: a combination that cannot be attained
questions.D: unemployment or inefficient use of resources
questions.explanation: Inside the frontier the economy is producing less than it could, so some resources are idle or wasted.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A combination of goods lying outside the production possibility curve is
questions.A: attainable only if some resources are left idle
questions.B: unattainable with present resources and technology
questions.C: the most efficient point for the economy
questions.D: attainable by reducing the output of one good
questions.explanation: Points beyond the frontier require more resources or better technology than the economy currently has.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following would shift a country's production possibility curve outwards?
questions.A: a decision to produce more of one good
questions.B: an increase in the prices of the two goods
questions.C: the discovery of new oil fields and improved technology
questions.D: a rise in the level of unemployment
questions.explanation: The frontier shifts outwards when the quantity or quality of resources rises or technology improves.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A student spends Saturday at a friend's party instead of working at a shop that would have paid her ₦3,000. The opportunity cost of attending the party is
questions.A: nothing, because the party was free
questions.B: the cost of transport to the party
questions.C: the food and drinks served at the party
questions.D: the ₦3,000 wage she gave up
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the best alternative forgone, here the ₦3,000 she could have earned.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The opportunity cost of using a resource is zero when the resource
questions.B: has no alternative use
questions.D: is used by many people at once
questions.explanation: If nothing else could have been done with the resource, nothing is sacrificed by using it; free goods are an example.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A production possibility curve that is a straight line shows that
questions.B: the opportunity cost rises as more is produced
questions.C: the opportunity cost of each good is constant
questions.D: one good cannot be produced at all
questions.explanation: A constant slope means a fixed amount of one good is given up for each extra unit of the other.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The concept of opportunity cost is useful to a government because it
questions.A: ensures that prices of goods remain stable
questions.B: guarantees that all projects will be completed on time
questions.C: removes the need to collect taxes from citizens
questions.D: helps it to allocate limited revenue among competing projects
questions.explanation: Weighing what must be given up for each project guides the choice among competing uses of scarce public funds.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A university degree costs ₦2 million in fees, and the student could have earned ₦1.5 million by working during the four years. The economic (opportunity) cost of the degree is
questions.B: ₦3.5 million
questions.D: ₦0.5 million
questions.explanation: Economic cost includes both the money paid out and the earnings forgone: 2 + 1.5 = ₦3.5 million.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Before going to the market, Bola writes down everything she needs and numbers the items from the most pressing to the least pressing. In economics her list is called
questions.B: a price list of goods in the market
questions.D: a demand schedule for the goods
questions.explanation: Consumers rank their wants so that the most pressing are satisfied first with the limited means available.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Ada earns ₦30,000 a month and ranks her wants as: rent ₦15,000, food ₦10,000, data ₦4,000, cinema ₦3,000 and new shoes ₦5,000. Satisfying her wants in that order, the number of wants she can fully satisfy this month is
questions.explanation: Rent + food + data = ₦29,000; the remaining ₦1,000 cannot fully pay for the cinema or the shoes.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The main reason a consumer draws up a scale of preference is that
questions.A: the government requires every consumer to do so
questions.B: her income cannot satisfy all her wants at once
questions.C: prices of goods are the same in all markets
questions.D: she has more money than she needs to spend
questions.explanation: Because means are limited relative to wants, ranking wants ensures the most important ones are met first.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A scale of preference helps a consumer to
questions.A: reduce the prices charged by sellers
questions.B: increase the amount of income she earns
questions.C: make a rational choice among competing wants
questions.D: avoid paying tax on the goods she buys
questions.explanation: It shows which wants to satisfy first and which to postpone, so spending is rational.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A business ranks its projects as: (1) buy a generator, (2) repaint the shop, (3) buy a delivery van, and has money for only one. It should undertake
questions.A: the generator; the van is its opportunity cost
questions.B: the van; the generator is its opportunity cost
questions.C: the repainting; the van is its opportunity cost
questions.D: the generator; the repainting is its opportunity cost
questions.explanation: The top-ranked project is chosen and the next best alternative forgone (repainting) is the opportunity cost.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following is TRUE of a scale of preference?
questions.A: it is the same for everyone with equal income
questions.B: it differs from one person to another
questions.C: it lists wants in the order they are remembered
questions.D: it is prepared only by governments and firms
questions.explanation: Tastes and circumstances differ, so two people with the same income may rank their wants differently.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: When a consumer's income rises while prices stay the same, her scale of preference
questions.B: must be discarded because it no longer applies
questions.C: allows more of the listed wants to be satisfied
questions.D: is no longer needed for rational choice
questions.explanation: The ranking may remain, but the higher income lets her move further down the list of wants.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The want placed at the top of a rational consumer's scale of preference is the one that
questions.A: was bought most recently by the consumer
questions.B: has the lowest price in the market
questions.C: is advertised most on radio and television
questions.D: gives the greatest satisfaction relative to the others
questions.explanation: Rational consumers rank wants by the satisfaction they give, not by price or advertising alone.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: In economics, production is said to be complete when the good
questions.B: reaches the final consumer
questions.D: is advertised on television
questions.explanation: Production includes distribution: it ends only when the good or service reaches the person who uses it.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A fisherman catching fish in the Lagos lagoon is engaged in
questions.B: secondary production
questions.D: indirect production
questions.explanation: Primary production extracts raw materials directly from nature (fishing, farming, mining).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Turning cassava into garri in a processing plant is an example of
questions.B: primary production
questions.D: secondary production
questions.explanation: Secondary production converts raw materials into finished or semi-finished goods.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A bank cashier and a lorry driver are both engaged in
questions.B: tertiary production
questions.D: direct production
questions.explanation: Both provide services (commercial and transport services), which is tertiary production.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Direct production differs from indirect production in that direct production
questions.A: involves the use of money as a medium of exchange
questions.B: always takes place in large factories
questions.C: is carried out to satisfy the producer's own wants
questions.D: requires a high degree of division of labour
questions.explanation: In direct (subsistence) production people make what they themselves consume; indirect production is for exchange.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The ultimate aim of production is to
questions.A: increase the population of a country
questions.B: provide employment for the citizens
questions.C: earn foreign exchange for the country
questions.D: create utility to satisfy human wants
questions.explanation: Goods and services are produced because they have utility, that is, the ability to satisfy wants.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A tailor who sews cloth into a dress creates
questions.B: form utility
questions.D: possession utility
questions.explanation: Changing the form of a material into a more useful product creates form utility.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A trader who buys yams cheaply in Benue and sells them in Lagos creates
questions.B: form utility
questions.D: service utility
questions.explanation: Moving goods from where they are plentiful to where they are wanted creates place utility.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Storing grains after the harvest and selling them during the dry season creates
questions.B: form utility
questions.D: time utility
questions.explanation: Making goods available when they are wanted, rather than when produced, creates time utility.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following is an example of tertiary production?
questions.A: a miner digging tin in Jos
questions.B: a lawyer defending a client in court
questions.D: a farmer growing rice in Kebbi
questions.explanation: Tertiary production consists of services; the others are primary (mining, farming) and secondary (weaving).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a stage of production?
questions.B: extraction of raw materials
questions.D: distribution of goods to consumers
questions.explanation: Consumption is the use of goods to satisfy wants; extraction, manufacturing and distribution are the stages of production.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Economists regard a retailer as a producer because he
questions.A: employs more workers than a farmer
questions.B: manufactures the goods that he sells
questions.C: fixes the prices of goods in the economy
questions.D: adds place and possession utility to goods
questions.explanation: By making goods available where and when consumers want them, the retailer adds utility, which is production.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A farmer who grows food crops only for his own family is engaged in
questions.B: subsistence production
questions.D: indirect production
questions.explanation: Producing for one's own consumption rather than for sale or exchange is subsistence (direct) production.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A landowner in Abuja receives ₦2 million a year from a company that uses his plot as a car park. In economics this payment is
questions.B: interest, the reward for capital
questions.D: wages, the reward for labour
questions.explanation: Payment for the use of land (a gift of nature) is rent; labour earns wages, capital interest and enterprise profit.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Capital as a factor of production is best described as
questions.A: any natural resource used in production
questions.B: the money a firm keeps in its bank account
questions.C: the shares issued by a public company
questions.D: man-made goods used to produce other goods
questions.explanation: Machines, tools, buildings and equipment are capital because they are produced goods used for further production.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: In economics, land includes
questions.A: only the soil used for growing crops
questions.B: all natural resources such as forests, rivers and minerals
questions.C: buildings and roads constructed on the soil
questions.D: the machines used to cultivate a farm
questions.explanation: Land covers all gifts of nature: the soil, minerals, water, forests and climate.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A distinguishing feature of land as a factor of production is that
questions.A: it can be moved from place to place
questions.B: its reward is called interest
questions.D: it is produced by human effort
questions.explanation: The total quantity of land cannot be increased by human effort, so it is fixed in supply and geographically immobile.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Labour differs from the other factors of production in that it
questions.A: can be stored and used at a later date
questions.B: is the only factor that receives a reward
questions.C: is never affected by changes in technology
questions.D: cannot be separated from the person who supplies it
questions.explanation: Labour is human effort; the worker must be present to supply it, and unused labour time is lost.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Interest is the reward for
questions.B: capital
questions.D: entrepreneurship
questions.explanation: Interest is paid for the use of capital (or the funds used to acquire it).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The entrepreneur differs from a salaried manager in that the entrepreneur
questions.B: supervises the daily work of employees
questions.C: bears the risk of the business
questions.D: cannot own shares in the business
questions.explanation: The entrepreneur organises the other factors and bears the uncertainty of loss; the manager is a paid employee.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: On a cocoa farm in Ondo State, the cocoa trees planted by the farmer are ______ while the soil is ______.
questions.B: land; capital
questions.D: capital; land
questions.explanation: The trees were produced by human effort to yield future output (capital); the soil is a gift of nature (land).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The efficiency of labour can be increased by
questions.A: reducing the wages paid to workers
questions.B: training, good health and better tools
questions.C: increasing the number of public holidays
questions.D: employing more workers on the same job
questions.explanation: Education, training, health, motivation and the quality of equipment all raise output per worker.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following would increase the supply of labour in a country?
questions.A: a rise in the school-leaving age
questions.B: a reduction in the normal working week
questions.C: an increase in the population of working age
questions.D: an increase in the emigration of young people
questions.explanation: More people of working age means more labour available; the other changes reduce the hours or numbers offered.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A teacher in Kano who accepts a teaching post in Ibadan shows
questions.B: occupational mobility of labour
questions.D: geographical mobility of labour
questions.explanation: Moving from one place to another in the same occupation is geographical mobility.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A bank cashier who retrains and becomes a nurse shows
questions.B: occupational mobility of labour
questions.D: immobility of labour
questions.explanation: Changing from one occupation to another is occupational mobility.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Wages differ between occupations mainly because of differences in
questions.A: the age of the workers employed in each occupation
questions.B: the number of public holidays enjoyed in each occupation
questions.C: the skill and training required and the demand for each type of labour
questions.D: the distance between the workers' homes and their offices
questions.explanation: Scarce skills that take long training and are in high demand command higher wages.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Division of labour is limited mainly by
questions.B: the number of public holidays
questions.D: the size of the market
questions.explanation: A producer can only split work into specialised tasks if the market is large enough to absorb the extra output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: An advantage of division of labour to a firm is that it
questions.A: makes workers independent of one another
questions.B: increases output per worker
questions.D: reduces the size of the market
questions.explanation: Practice makes workers more skilful and less time is wasted moving between tasks, so productivity rises.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A disadvantage of division of labour to the worker is
questions.A: a fall in the total output of the factory
questions.B: an increase in the time taken to learn the job
questions.C: monotony from repeating one task all day
questions.D: the need to buy his own tools and machines
questions.explanation: Doing the same small task repeatedly becomes boring and can reduce job satisfaction.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A country that concentrates on producing cocoa and imports most other goods is practising
questions.B: division of labour by process
questions.D: international specialisation
questions.explanation: When countries concentrate on the goods they produce best and trade for others, they specialise internationally.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Division of labour makes the use of machines possible because
questions.A: workers no longer need to be trained
questions.B: each task is broken into simple, repetitive operations
questions.C: machines are cheaper than human labour
questions.D: the market for the product becomes smaller
questions.explanation: Simple, repetitive operations can be mechanised more easily than a complex job done by one craftsman.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Specialisation by a country in one or two export crops is risky because
questions.A: farmers will refuse to grow any other crop
questions.B: the country cannot use money as a medium of exchange
questions.C: a fall in the world price of the crops hurts the whole economy
questions.D: the crops cannot be transported to other countries
questions.explanation: Over-dependence on a few products exposes the economy to price and demand shocks in the world market.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Division of labour increases the need for
questions.B: subsistence farming
questions.D: a medium of exchange
questions.explanation: Specialised workers produce more than they need of one thing and must exchange the surplus, which money makes easy.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A one-man barbing salon cannot practise division of labour mainly because
questions.A: barbing cannot be broken into separate tasks
questions.B: the scale of the business is too small
questions.D: customers prefer to be served by one person
questions.explanation: Division of labour requires enough workers and enough work to split; a one-man business has neither.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Adam Smith used the example of a pin factory to show that
questions.B: pins are the most important manufactured good
questions.C: division of labour greatly increases output
questions.D: workers should own the factories they work in
questions.explanation: Smith observed that ten specialised workers made far more pins per day than ten working separately.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A worker who spends years fixing only car tyres on an assembly line and can no longer build a complete car has suffered
questions.B: occupational mobility
questions.D: loss of craftsmanship
questions.explanation: Narrow specialisation can destroy the all-round skill of the craftsman who once made the whole product.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Specialisation by process in a car assembly plant makes workers
questions.A: independent, so each can finish a car alone
questions.B: interdependent, so a stoppage in one section can halt production
questions.C: less skilled in the tasks they perform
questions.D: unwilling to use machines in their work
questions.explanation: Each section depends on the output of the previous one, so a strike or breakdown in one section affects all.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: In a free market economy, the basic economic problems are solved through
questions.B: central planning
questions.D: custom and tradition
questions.explanation: Prices set by demand and supply signal what to produce, how to produce and for whom.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The main feature of a capitalist economy is
questions.B: state ownership of all industries
questions.C: the absence of money and prices
questions.D: private ownership of the means of production
questions.explanation: In capitalism individuals own resources and firms and make decisions in pursuit of profit.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: An advantage of a centrally planned economy is that
questions.A: consumers have the widest choice of goods
questions.B: resources can be directed to socially desirable goods
questions.C: prices respond quickly to changes in demand
questions.D: individuals are free to set up any business
questions.explanation: The planning authority can ensure essential goods and services are produced even if they are not the most profitable.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A disadvantage of the free market economy is that it
questions.A: gives consumers no freedom of choice
questions.B: removes the profit motive from producers
questions.C: may neglect the provision of public goods
questions.D: requires a large planning bureaucracy
questions.explanation: Private firms cannot profitably supply goods like street lighting and defence, so markets under-provide them.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Street lighting is usually provided by the government rather than by private firms because
questions.A: it is consumed only by the very poor in society
questions.B: it is more expensive than any other public service
questions.C: private firms are not allowed to own electric bulbs
questions.D: nobody can be excluded from enjoying it once it is provided
questions.explanation: Non-excludability means private firms cannot charge users, so public goods would not be supplied by the market.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: In a mixed economy, the government intervenes in the market mainly to
questions.B: correct the failures of the free market
questions.C: fix the prices of all goods and services
questions.D: prevent consumers from saving money
questions.explanation: Mixed economies combine private enterprise with state action to provide public goods, regulate monopolies and redistribute income.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following countries operated a centrally planned economy for most of the twentieth century?
questions.B: the United States
questions.D: Nigeria
questions.explanation: The Soviet Union's economy was directed by state plans from the 1920s until its collapse in 1991.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A characteristic of a socialist economy is that
questions.A: consumers decide what is produced through their spending
questions.B: firms compete freely to maximise their profits
questions.C: the means of production belong to private individuals
questions.D: prices are fixed by the state rather than by demand and supply
questions.explanation: Under socialism the state owns the major means of production and sets prices and output targets.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: In a traditional (subsistence) economy, what to produce is decided mainly by
questions.B: custom and tradition
questions.D: multinational companies
questions.explanation: People produce what their ancestors produced, using traditional methods, largely for their own consumption.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Consumer sovereignty means that
questions.A: consumers are members of the country's parliament
questions.B: the government protects consumers from high prices
questions.C: consumers' spending decisions determine what is produced
questions.D: producers decide what consumers should buy
questions.explanation: In a market economy producers respond to the pattern of consumer demand, so consumers ultimately direct production.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Nigeria's sale of state-owned enterprises such as NITEL and the power companies to private investors moved the economy
questions.A: away from private ownership of firms
questions.B: towards a centrally planned system
questions.D: towards greater reliance on the market
questions.explanation: Privatisation transfers production decisions from the state to private owners guided by the market.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Adam Smith's "invisible hand" refers to
questions.A: the secret control of the economy by the government
questions.B: the way self-interest in free markets promotes the good of society
questions.C: the influence of foreign firms on a nation's economy
questions.D: the power of trade unions to fix wages
questions.explanation: Smith argued that individuals pursuing their own gain are led, as if by an invisible hand, to serve society through the market.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Effective demand refers to
questions.A: the desire for a good that a consumer cannot afford
questions.B: the total quantity of a good produced in the economy
questions.C: the desire for a good backed by the ability and willingness to pay
questions.D: the amount of a good that the government supplies
questions.explanation: In economics, demand means desire backed by purchasing power at a given price and time.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A trader noticed that whenever she reduced the price of her oranges, customers bought more of them. This everyday observation illustrates the law of demand, which states that, other things being equal,
questions.B: the higher the price, the higher the quantity demanded
questions.C: quantity demanded does not change with price
questions.D: the higher the price, the lower the quantity demanded
questions.explanation: Price and quantity demanded are inversely related, giving a downward-sloping demand curve.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A movement along the demand curve for garri is caused by
questions.B: a change in the price of garri
questions.C: a change in the price of rice
questions.D: a change in consumers' tastes
questions.explanation: Only a change in the good's own price moves along the curve; other factors shift the whole curve.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following will shift the demand curve for a brand of powdered milk to the right?
questions.A: a fall in the price of a rival brand
questions.B: a fall in the price of the milk itself
questions.D: a health report linking the brand to illness
questions.explanation: Higher income raises demand for a normal good at every price; the own-price change is a movement, the others reduce demand.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Petrol and cars are ______ goods, so a large rise in the price of petrol will ______ the demand for cars.
questions.B: substitute; increase
questions.D: complementary; reduce
questions.explanation: Goods used together are complements: dearer petrol makes running a car costlier and reduces demand for cars.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: If the price of tea rises sharply, the demand for coffee is likely to
questions.A: decrease, because the two are complements
questions.B: increase, because the two are substitutes
questions.C: remain unchanged, because they are unrelated
questions.D: fall to zero, because consumers switch to tea
questions.explanation: Tea and coffee satisfy the same want; when one becomes dearer, consumers switch to the other.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A good whose demand rises when consumers' incomes rise is
questions.B: an inferior good
questions.D: a free good
questions.explanation: Normal goods have positive income elasticity of demand.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: As workers in a town received higher salaries, their purchases of garri fell while purchases of rice rose. For these workers, garri is
questions.B: a normal good
questions.D: an inferior good
questions.explanation: Demand for an inferior good falls as income rises because consumers switch to preferred alternatives.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A wealthy man buys a very expensive wristwatch precisely because its high price displays his status. The watch is
questions.B: an ostentatious (Veblen) good
questions.D: a producer good
questions.explanation: For goods of ostentation, a higher price increases their appeal, an exception to the law of demand.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The demand for bricklayers depends on the demand for new houses. The demand for bricklayers is
questions.B: joint demand
questions.D: competitive demand
questions.explanation: Factors of production are demanded not for their own sake but for the goods they help to produce.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The demand for exercise books and biros together at the start of a school term is an example of
questions.B: composite demand
questions.D: joint demand
questions.explanation: Joint (complementary) demand arises when goods are wanted together to satisfy one want.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Palm oil is demanded for cooking, soap-making and margarine production. The demand for palm oil is
questions.B: composite demand
questions.D: competitive demand
questions.explanation: Composite demand is demand for a good that has several different uses.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Consumers choosing between two rival brands of instant noodles illustrate
questions.B: joint demand
questions.D: derived demand
questions.explanation: When goods are substitutes for each other, their demands are competitive.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Other things being equal, a fall in the price of a good leads to
questions.A: a shift of the demand curve to the left
questions.B: a shift of the demand curve to the right
questions.C: a contraction of demand along the same curve
questions.D: an extension of demand along the same curve
questions.explanation: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the curve; a fall in price extends quantity demanded.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The market demand curve for a good is obtained by
questions.A: multiplying the price by the number of consumers
questions.B: adding the quantities demanded by all consumers at each price
questions.C: adding the prices paid by all the consumers
questions.D: taking the demand of the largest single buyer
questions.explanation: Market demand is the horizontal summation of individual demand curves.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following is an exception to the law of demand?
questions.A: goods bought in smaller quantities when income falls
questions.B: goods whose demand falls when their prices rise
questions.C: goods bought in larger quantities because their prices are expected to rise further
questions.D: goods whose demand rises when the price of a substitute rises
questions.explanation: When consumers expect further price rises, they may buy more as price rises; Giffen and ostentatious goods are other exceptions.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The law of supply states that, other things being equal,
questions.B: less is supplied at higher prices than at lower prices
questions.C: supply is fixed regardless of price
questions.D: more is supplied at higher prices than at lower prices
questions.explanation: Higher prices make production more profitable, so producers offer more; the supply curve slopes upwards.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following will shift the supply curve of bread to the right?
questions.A: a rise in the price of bread
questions.B: a fall in the price of flour
questions.C: an increase in the wages of bakers
questions.D: a new tax on each loaf of bread
questions.explanation: Cheaper inputs lower costs so more is supplied at every price; the own-price change is a movement along the curve.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: On a market day, the supply of fresh tomatoes already brought to the market is
questions.A: increased easily if the price rises
questions.B: perfectly elastic at the ruling price
questions.D: determined by the number of buyers
questions.explanation: Perishable goods already on sale cannot be increased or withheld for long, so supply is fixed for that day.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Beef and hides are produced together from cattle. Their supply is
questions.B: competitive supply
questions.D: joint supply
questions.explanation: Joint supply occurs when the production of one good automatically produces another.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A farmer can use his land either for maize or for beans. The supply of the two crops is
questions.B: competitive
questions.D: complementary
questions.explanation: When the same resources can produce either good, more of one means less of the other: competitive supply.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A new tax on each bag of cement produced will
questions.A: cause a movement down the supply curve
questions.B: shift the supply curve of cement to the right
questions.C: shift the supply curve of cement to the left
questions.D: leave the supply curve unchanged
questions.explanation: The tax raises the cost of supplying each bag, so less is offered at every price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A government subsidy on fertiliser will most likely
questions.A: leave the supply of fertiliser unchanged
questions.B: reduce the supply of fertiliser and raise its price
questions.C: reduce the demand for fertiliser by farmers
questions.D: increase the supply of fertiliser and lower its price
questions.explanation: A subsidy lowers producers' costs, shifting supply to the right and reducing the market price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: An improvement in technology in the poultry industry will
questions.A: reduce the quantity of eggs supplied at every price
questions.B: increase the quantity of eggs supplied at every price
questions.C: shift the demand curve for eggs to the left
questions.D: have no effect on the supply of eggs
questions.explanation: Better technology lowers unit costs, so producers can offer more at each price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A movement along the supply curve of yam is caused by a change in
questions.B: the cost of fertiliser
questions.D: the price of cassava
questions.explanation: Only the good's own price causes a movement along its supply curve; other factors shift the curve.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Quantity supplied is the amount of a good that producers
questions.A: would like to sell if the price were much higher
questions.B: have produced in total since the firm was established
questions.C: keep in their warehouses for future sale
questions.D: are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price and time
questions.explanation: Supply, like demand, is defined at a specific price over a specific period.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: An increase in supply means that
questions.A: the price of the good has risen
questions.B: more is offered for sale at every price
questions.C: producers have moved up the supply curve
questions.D: the quantity demanded has increased
questions.explanation: An increase in supply is a rightward shift of the whole curve, not a movement along it.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A backward-bending supply curve is associated with the supply of
questions.B: land
questions.D: agricultural produce
questions.explanation: Beyond a certain wage, workers may prefer more leisure and offer fewer hours, so the labour supply curve bends backwards.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A fall in the price of cocoa, other things being equal, leads to
questions.A: an increase in the supply of cocoa
questions.B: an extension in the quantity of cocoa supplied
questions.C: a rightward shift of the cocoa supply curve
questions.D: a contraction in the quantity of cocoa supplied
questions.explanation: Lower prices make production less profitable, so quantity supplied falls along the same curve.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Rice traders who expect the price of rice to rise sharply next month are likely to
questions.B: withhold some stock from the market now
questions.C: reduce the price of rice now
questions.D: import less rice next month
questions.explanation: Expectations of higher future prices reduce current supply as sellers hold back stock to sell later.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The equilibrium price of a good is the price at which
questions.A: sellers make the largest possible profit
questions.B: the government fixes the price of the good
questions.D: buyers are willing to pay the highest price
questions.explanation: At equilibrium there is neither shortage nor surplus, so the price has no tendency to change.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: When the market price of a good is below its equilibrium level, there is
questions.A: excess supply, which pushes the price up
questions.B: excess supply, which pushes the price down
questions.C: equilibrium, so the price stays the same
questions.D: excess demand, which pushes the price up
questions.explanation: At a low price buyers want more than sellers offer; competition among buyers bids the price up.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The demand and supply functions for a good are Qd = 60 − 2P and Qs = 3P − 15. The equilibrium price is
questions.explanation: Set 60 − 2P = 3P − 15, so 5P = 75 and P = 15.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: If Qd = 60 − 2P and Qs = 3P − 15, the equilibrium quantity is
questions.B: 45 units
questions.D: 60 units

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A government fixes a minimum wage above the equilibrium wage. The likely result in the labour market is
questions.A: a rise in the demand for labour
questions.B: a shortage of labour
questions.D: a surplus of labour (unemployment)
questions.explanation: A price floor above equilibrium raises the quantity of labour supplied and reduces the quantity demanded.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A state government fixes a maximum price for cooking gas well below the market equilibrium. Apart from shortages, a likely consequence is
questions.A: a surplus of cement in the market
questions.B: the emergence of a black market
questions.C: a fall in the demand for cement
questions.D: an increase in the supply of cement
questions.explanation: A price ceiling creates a shortage, and some buyers will pay more than the legal price illegally.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: An increase in demand for a good, with supply unchanged, leads to
questions.A: a rise in price and a fall in quantity
questions.B: a fall in both equilibrium price and quantity
questions.C: a rise in both equilibrium price and quantity
questions.D: a fall in price and a rise in quantity
questions.explanation: The demand curve shifts right along an upward-sloping supply curve, so price and quantity both rise.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: An increase in supply with demand unchanged will
questions.A: lower both the equilibrium price and quantity
questions.B: raise the equilibrium price and lower the equilibrium quantity
questions.C: raise both the equilibrium price and quantity
questions.D: lower the equilibrium price and raise the equilibrium quantity
questions.explanation: A rightward shift of supply along a downward-sloping demand curve reduces price and increases quantity.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: If demand and supply of a good both increase by the same proportion, the equilibrium
questions.A: price rises while the quantity stays the same
questions.B: quantity rises while the price stays the same
questions.D: price rises and the quantity falls
questions.explanation: Equal rightward shifts of both curves leave the price unchanged but raise the quantity traded.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Given Qd = 50 − P and Qs = 2P − 10, at a price of ₦25 the market has
questions.B: a shortage of 15 units
questions.D: equilibrium
questions.explanation: At P = 25, Qd = 25 and Qs = 40, so 15 units are unsold.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The price system rations scarce goods by
questions.A: allowing the government to decide who gets them
questions.B: sharing them equally among all consumers
questions.C: giving them first to those who queue longest
questions.D: allocating them to those willing and able to pay the price
questions.explanation: When a good is scarce its price rises until only those who can and will pay obtain it.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The government fixes the pump price of petrol at ₦600 per litre when the market equilibrium is ₦900. The likely effects are
questions.A: a surplus of petrol at filling stations
questions.B: long queues, shortages and a black market
questions.C: a fall in the demand for petrol
questions.D: an increase in the supply of petrol
questions.explanation: A maximum price below equilibrium causes excess demand; rationing by queues and illegal sales above the fixed price follow.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A rise in the cost of production of a good, with demand unchanged, will lead to
questions.A: a higher equilibrium price and a higher equilibrium quantity
questions.B: a lower equilibrium price and a higher equilibrium quantity
questions.C: a higher equilibrium price and a lower equilibrium quantity
questions.D: no change in the equilibrium price or quantity
questions.explanation: Higher costs shift supply to the left: price rises and quantity falls.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The demand and supply of a good are Qd = 100 − 5P and Qs = 5P. The total revenue of sellers at equilibrium is
questions.explanation: 100 − 5P = 5P gives P = 10 and Q = 50; revenue = 10 × 50 = ₦500.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A shop raised the price of a sachet of detergent from ₦40 to ₦50 and its weekly sales fell from 200 to 170 sachets. Using original values, the price elasticity of demand is

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The price elasticity of demand for a good is 2. If its price falls by 5%, the quantity demanded will
questions.B: rise by 2.5%
questions.D: rise by 5%
questions.explanation: %ΔQ = elasticity × %ΔP = 2 × 5% = 10%, in the opposite direction to the price change.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A 20% rise in the price of a good leaves the seller's total revenue unchanged. The demand for the good is
questions.B: perfectly inelastic
questions.D: unitary elastic
questions.explanation: When demand is unit elastic, the percentage fall in quantity equals the percentage rise in price, so revenue is constant.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A perfectly inelastic demand curve is
questions.B: a vertical straight line
questions.D: an upward-sloping curve
questions.explanation: Quantity demanded does not change at all when price changes, so the curve is vertical.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A perfectly elastic demand curve is
questions.B: a vertical straight line
questions.D: a curve sloping upwards
questions.explanation: Buyers take any quantity at one price but nothing at a higher price, so the curve is horizontal.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The demand for a good is likely to be more elastic when
questions.B: the good is a necessity of life
questions.C: the good takes a tiny share of income
questions.D: the good has many close substitutes
questions.explanation: Availability of substitutes makes consumers respond strongly to a change in price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: When the price of a good rose by 10%, the quantity supplied rose by 25%. The price elasticity of supply is
questions.explanation: Elasticity of supply = 25% ÷ 10% = 2.5, so supply is elastic.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Supply is usually more elastic in the long run than in the short run because
questions.A: consumers have more time to change their tastes
questions.B: prices always rise in the long run
questions.C: producers can adjust all their factors of production
questions.D: the government removes all taxes in the long run
questions.explanation: Given time, firms can build new plants and new firms can enter, so output responds more to price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The cross elasticity of demand between bread and butter is −0.8. The two goods are
questions.B: substitutes
questions.D: complements
questions.explanation: A negative cross elasticity means a rise in the price of one reduces the demand for the other: they are used together.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: When consumers' incomes rose by 10%, the demand for garri fell by 4%. The income elasticity of demand for garri is
questions.B: −0.4, so garri is an inferior good
questions.D: 2.5, so garri is a normal good
questions.explanation: Income elasticity = −4% ÷ 10% = −0.4; a negative value identifies an inferior good.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A good whose income elasticity of demand is greater than 1 is
questions.B: a necessity
questions.D: a Giffen good
questions.explanation: Demand for luxuries rises more than proportionately when income rises.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: After a bumper harvest, tomato farmers found their total revenue fell even though they sold more. This is because the demand for tomatoes is
questions.B: price elastic
questions.D: price inelastic
questions.explanation: With inelastic demand the large price fall needed to sell the extra output reduces total revenue.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A government that wants to raise the most revenue from an indirect tax should tax goods whose demand is
questions.B: price inelastic
questions.D: highly income elastic
questions.explanation: When demand is inelastic, the tax raises price without greatly reducing the quantity bought, so revenue is high.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: On a straight-line downward-sloping demand curve, demand is unitary elastic
questions.A: where the curve meets the price axis
questions.B: at every point on the curve
questions.C: at the midpoint of the curve
questions.D: where the curve meets the quantity axis
questions.explanation: Elasticity falls from infinity at the price axis to zero at the quantity axis, passing through 1 at the midpoint.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The demand for petrol is inelastic in the short run mainly because
questions.A: the government controls the number of petrol stations
questions.B: petrol is very cheap compared with other goods
questions.D: motorists cannot quickly change their vehicles or travel habits
questions.explanation: In the short run there are few substitutes and consumers need time to adjust, so quantity demanded responds little to price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A seller raised the price of a good from ₦100 to ₦120 and total revenue rose from ₦50,000 to ₦54,000. The demand for the good is
questions.B: price inelastic
questions.D: perfectly elastic
questions.explanation: Total revenue rises when price rises only if demand is inelastic.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following goods is likely to have the LEAST elastic demand?
questions.B: a particular brand of biscuit
questions.D: a new private car
questions.explanation: Salt is a cheap necessity with no close substitute, so its quantity demanded hardly responds to price; the others are luxuries or have many substitutes.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Utility in economics means
questions.A: the profit a producer makes from a good
questions.B: the usefulness of a good to the whole society
questions.C: the price a consumer pays for a good
questions.D: the satisfaction derived from consuming a good or service
questions.explanation: Utility is subjective satisfaction; a good has utility if it satisfies a want, whether or not it is useful.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Marginal utility is
questions.A: the total satisfaction from all units consumed
questions.B: the extra satisfaction from consuming one more unit of a good
questions.C: the satisfaction from the first unit consumed
questions.D: the average satisfaction per unit consumed
questions.explanation: MU = change in total utility ÷ change in quantity consumed.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that as a consumer consumes more units of a good,
questions.A: the price of the good keeps falling
questions.B: total satisfaction falls from the first unit
questions.C: the additional satisfaction from each extra unit falls
questions.D: the additional satisfaction from each unit rises
questions.explanation: Successive units add less and less to total utility, other things being equal.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: When total utility is at its maximum, marginal utility is
questions.B: at its maximum
questions.D: zero
questions.explanation: Total utility stops rising when the extra unit adds nothing; beyond that point MU becomes negative.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A cup of rice gives a consumer 30 utils and costs ₦150; a cup of beans gives 40 utils and costs ₦250. To increase total satisfaction with the same money, the consumer should buy
questions.B: more rice and less beans
questions.D: only beans
questions.explanation: MU per naira: rice 30/150 = 0.2, beans 40/250 = 0.16; shifting spending towards rice raises total utility until the ratios are equal.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Water is essential to life yet cheap, while diamonds are unnecessary yet very expensive. This paradox of value is explained by
questions.B: total utility
questions.D: the cost of production
questions.explanation: Price reflects marginal, not total, utility: water is abundant so its marginal utility is low, diamonds are scarce so theirs is high.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Consumer surplus is
questions.A: the profit a seller makes on each unit sold
questions.B: the extra goods a consumer buys when prices fall
questions.C: the money a consumer has left after buying all his needs
questions.D: the difference between what a consumer is willing to pay and what he actually pays
questions.explanation: It measures the benefit consumers gain from paying a market price lower than their maximum willingness to pay.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Ngozi was willing to pay ₦1,200 for a textbook but bought it for ₦900. Her consumer surplus is
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus = willingness to pay − price paid = 1,200 − 900 = ₦300.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: An indifference curve shows
questions.A: the combinations of two goods a consumer can afford
questions.B: the quantities of a good bought at different prices
questions.C: combinations of two goods that give the consumer equal satisfaction
questions.D: how total utility changes as consumption rises
questions.explanation: The consumer is indifferent between all the combinations on one curve.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A consumer's budget line shifts outwards, parallel to the old one, when
questions.A: the prices of both goods rise proportionately
questions.B: the price of one good rises
questions.C: her tastes change in favour of one good
questions.D: her income rises while prices remain unchanged
questions.explanation: Higher income with constant prices lets her buy more of both goods, so the whole line moves out.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Measuring satisfaction in units called utils is the ______ approach to utility.
questions.B: ordinal
questions.D: indifference
questions.explanation: The cardinal approach assumes utility can be measured in numbers; the ordinal approach only ranks preferences.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A rational consumer buying a single good will stop buying additional units when
questions.A: the marginal utility of the good, in money terms, equals its price
questions.B: total utility begins to rise
questions.C: the marginal utility of the good is at its maximum
questions.D: the price of the good begins to fall
questions.explanation: Buying continues while each extra unit is worth at least its price; the last unit bought is worth exactly the price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: When the price of beef falls and a consumer buys more beef in place of the relatively dearer fish, this is the
questions.A: substitution effect of the price change
questions.B: income effect of the price change
questions.D: paradox of value
questions.explanation: A fall in relative price leads consumers to substitute the cheaper good for the dearer one.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A firm differs from an industry in that a firm is
questions.A: a single unit of production under one ownership or management
questions.B: a group of producers making similar products
questions.C: any market in which goods are exchanged
questions.D: the whole of the economy's manufacturing sector
questions.explanation: An industry is made up of all the firms producing the same or similar products.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The law of diminishing returns operates in the short run because
questions.A: at least one factor of production is fixed
questions.B: all factors of production can be varied
questions.C: the firm can change its scale of operation
questions.D: prices of inputs rise as output rises
questions.explanation: Adding more of a variable factor to a fixed factor eventually yields smaller additions to output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Employing a fourth worker raised a workshop's output from 60 to 84 units, and a fifth raised it to 100 units. The marginal product of the fifth worker is
questions.B: 24 units
questions.D: 100 units
questions.explanation: MP = change in total product = 100 − 84 = 16 units, less than the fourth worker's 24: diminishing returns have set in.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Five workers in a bakery produce 100 loaves a day. The average product of labour is
questions.B: 100 loaves
questions.D: 500 loaves
questions.explanation: Average product = total product ÷ number of workers = 100 ÷ 5 = 20 loaves.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: In the short run, a firm's fixed factor is most likely to be its
questions.B: raw materials
questions.D: electricity consumption
questions.explanation: Buildings and heavy plant cannot be changed quickly; materials, casual labour and power vary with output.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The long run in the theory of production is the period in which
questions.A: all factors of production can be varied
questions.B: at least one factor is fixed
questions.C: no new firms can enter the industry
questions.D: prices of all inputs are constant
questions.explanation: In the long run a firm can change its plant size and scale, and firms can enter or leave the industry.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A large flour mill buys wheat in bulk at a discount and spreads its advertising cost over millions of bags. These are examples of
questions.B: external economies of scale
questions.D: diminishing returns
questions.explanation: Cost advantages that arise from the growth of the firm itself are internal economies of scale.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A shoe firm in Aba benefits from the pool of skilled shoemakers and leather suppliers that have grown up in the town. This is an example of
questions.B: internal economies of scale
questions.D: internal diseconomies of scale
questions.explanation: Advantages that come from the growth of the whole industry in an area, not from the firm's own size, are external economies.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: As a company grew very large, decisions became slow, communication broke down and unit costs began to rise. The firm was experiencing
questions.B: economies of scale
questions.D: external economies
questions.explanation: Beyond the optimum size, management problems raise average cost; these are internal diseconomies of scale.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A firm earning normal profit is one whose total revenue
questions.A: just covers total cost including the reward of the entrepreneur
questions.B: exceeds total cost by a very large margin
questions.C: covers variable cost but not fixed cost
questions.D: is less than the wages paid to its workers
questions.explanation: Normal profit is the minimum return that keeps the entrepreneur in the industry and is counted as a cost.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The optimum size of a firm is the size at which it
questions.A: produces at the lowest average cost
questions.B: employs the largest number of workers
questions.D: has the largest share of the market
questions.explanation: At the optimum, all economies of scale have been reaped and diseconomies have not yet set in.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Many small firms survive alongside large ones in Nigeria mainly because
questions.A: they serve small local markets and offer personal services
questions.B: the law forbids firms from growing beyond a certain size
questions.C: large firms always have higher costs than small ones
questions.D: small firms pay no taxes to the government
questions.explanation: Where the market is small or personal attention matters, the advantages of large scale are limited.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The total product of a firm with 10 workers is 200 units. Average product per worker is
questions.B: 10 units
questions.D: 2,000 units
questions.explanation: AP = TP ÷ L = 200 ÷ 10 = 20 units.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Fixed costs are costs that
questions.A: do not vary with output in the short run
questions.B: rise as output rises
questions.C: are paid only when the firm produces
questions.D: fall when output increases
questions.explanation: Rent, insurance and interest on loans must be paid even when output is zero.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following is a variable cost for a pure-water factory?
questions.B: the rent of the factory premises
questions.C: the insurance premium on the building
questions.D: the salary of the general manager
questions.explanation: The cost of sachets rises directly with the number of bags produced; the others are fixed in the short run.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A firm's total fixed cost is ₦40,000 and its average variable cost is ₦50 when it produces 1,000 units. Its total cost is

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Average fixed cost falls continuously as output rises because
questions.A: the same fixed cost is spread over more units
questions.B: fixed cost falls as the firm grows
questions.C: variable cost falls as output rises
questions.D: the firm receives discounts on rent
questions.explanation: AFC = TFC ÷ output; a constant numerator divided by a rising output gives a falling value.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A block-moulding business found that its weekly total cost rose from ₦300,000 to ₦324,000 when it increased output from 100 to 106 blocks. The marginal cost per block is

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A trader uses her own shop for her business instead of renting it out for ₦200,000 a year. The ₦200,000 is
questions.B: an explicit cost
questions.D: a sunk cost
questions.explanation: Implicit costs are the opportunity costs of using the owner's own resources; no money payment is made.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Explicit costs are
questions.A: actual money payments made to outsiders for inputs
questions.B: the opportunity costs of the owner's own resources
questions.C: costs that cannot be recovered once incurred
questions.D: costs that do not change with output
questions.explanation: Wages, rent and payments for materials are explicit (accounting) costs.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Money already spent on an advertising campaign that failed cannot be recovered. It is
questions.B: a variable cost
questions.D: a marginal cost
questions.explanation: Sunk costs have already been incurred and should not affect future decisions.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The marginal cost curve cuts the average total cost curve at
questions.A: the minimum point of the average total cost curve
questions.B: the maximum point of the average total cost curve
questions.C: the point where average fixed cost is zero
questions.D: the point where total cost is lowest
questions.explanation: When MC is below ATC it pulls ATC down; when above, it pushes ATC up; so they meet at ATC's minimum.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The U-shape of the short-run average cost curve is explained by
questions.B: economies of scale
questions.D: changes in the prices of inputs
questions.explanation: Average cost first falls as the fixed factor is used more fully, then rises when diminishing returns set in.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The downward-sloping part of a firm's long-run average cost curve is due to
questions.B: diminishing returns
questions.D: rising input prices
questions.explanation: As the firm expands its scale, technical, managerial and financial economies lower unit cost.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: When marginal cost is below average variable cost, average variable cost is
questions.B: rising
questions.D: at its minimum
questions.explanation: An extra unit costing less than the current average pulls the average down.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: At an output of 50 units a firm's average total cost is ₦120 and its average fixed cost is ₦40. Its total variable cost is

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A firm's total revenue is ₦500,000, its explicit costs are ₦350,000 and its implicit costs are ₦100,000. Its economic profit is
questions.explanation: Economic profit = TR − (explicit + implicit costs) = 500,000 − 450,000 = ₦50,000; accounting profit would be ₦150,000.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A factory discharges waste into a river, killing the fish on which a nearby village depends. The loss suffered by the village is
questions.B: a private cost of the factory
questions.C: a fixed cost of the factory
questions.D: an implicit cost of the village
questions.explanation: Costs imposed on third parties who are not part of the transaction are external (social) costs.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A trader sells 200 units of a good at ₦150 each. Her total revenue is
questions.explanation: Total revenue = price × quantity = 150 × 200 = ₦30,000.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Average revenue is always equal to
questions.B: marginal revenue
questions.D: marginal cost
questions.explanation: AR = TR ÷ Q = (P × Q) ÷ Q = P.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Under monopoly, marginal revenue is less than average revenue because
questions.A: the firm must lower its price to sell more units
questions.B: the firm faces a horizontal demand curve
questions.C: the monopolist's costs rise with output
questions.D: the government fixes the monopolist's price
questions.explanation: Selling an extra unit means cutting the price on all units, so the revenue added is less than the new price.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Normal profit is
questions.A: the minimum return needed to keep the entrepreneur in the business
questions.B: the profit earned when total revenue equals variable cost
questions.C: any profit above the average for the industry
questions.D: the profit declared to tax authorities
questions.explanation: Normal profit is treated as a cost of production because without it the entrepreneur would leave.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A firm earns supernormal (abnormal) profit when
questions.A: total revenue exceeds total cost including normal profit
questions.B: total revenue just equals total cost
questions.C: average revenue equals average variable cost
questions.D: marginal revenue is zero
questions.explanation: Supernormal profit is the excess over the normal profit already counted in costs.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A firm's total revenue is ₦1,200,000 and its total cost is ₦950,000. Its profit is

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A bakery's weekly revenue rose from ₦80,000 to ₦84,000 when its sales rose from 400 to 410 loaves. The marginal revenue per loaf is

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A firm whose total revenue is exactly equal to its total cost is
questions.B: making a loss
questions.D: shutting down
questions.explanation: At the break-even point the firm covers all its costs, including normal profit, but earns nothing extra.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Profit is the reward for
questions.B: the use of land
questions.D: the use of borrowed capital
questions.explanation: The entrepreneur who organises production and bears its risks receives profit, which may be negative.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: When demand is price elastic, a fall in price will
questions.B: reduce total revenue
questions.D: reduce the quantity sold
questions.explanation: With elastic demand the percentage rise in quantity exceeds the percentage fall in price, so revenue rises.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A monopolist's total revenue is at its maximum where
questions.B: marginal revenue equals price
questions.D: marginal cost is zero
questions.explanation: Total revenue stops rising when an extra unit adds nothing to it, i.e. MR = 0 (demand is unit elastic there).

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: A firm has fixed costs of ₦100,000, sells each unit for ₦500 and incurs a variable cost of ₦300 per unit. Its break-even output is
questions.B: 200 units
questions.D: 1,000 units
questions.explanation: Each unit contributes 500 − 300 = ₦200 towards fixed cost; 100,000 ÷ 200 = 500 units.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Which of the following would reduce a firm's profit without any change in its revenue?
questions.A: a rise in the price of its raw materials
questions.B: a rise in the price of its product
questions.C: an increase in the quantity it sells
questions.D: a fall in the wages it pays
questions.explanation: Higher input prices raise total cost; with revenue unchanged, profit falls.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: Under perfect competition an individual firm is a price taker because it
questions.A: produces a negligible share of total market output
questions.B: is the only seller of the product in the whole market
questions.C: sells a product that differs from those of its rivals
questions.D: can fix any price it likes for the product it sells
questions.explanation: One firm's output is too small to influence the market price, so it must accept the price set by the market.

questions.subject: Economics
questions.q: The demand curve facing a firm in a perfectly competitive market is
